case_study_insert.main_stem: Threadwind Fashion (TWF) is a partnership in the knitwear e-commerce retail sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2011 by Beatrix Fenn, the business sells own-brand knitwear to consumers through its online store and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. TWF plans to invest $560,000 in a new e-commerce returns and yarn-refurbishment hub, financed by a $360,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $144,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.20 a unit and a selling price of $11.00, and currently produces 78,000 units a year. TWF faces two operational problems: pilling-related quality complaints have risen to 38 a month and absenteeism in the packing team has reached 8.5%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: E-commerce Quality Report â€” Q3 2025: The knitwear store fulfilled 16,800 orders, with a pilling-related defect rate of 3.4% and 38 quality complaints per month, up from 22. Median delivery time is 3.1 days. A survey of 640 online knitwear buyers found that 66% would pay up to $0.70 more for guaranteed non-pilling yarn, and 54% read online reviews before ordering. A training check shows 14 of 52 packing staff have not been inducted on the new returns scanner; a short e-learning module costs $60 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.80 to $13.50 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills in warehousing and fulfilment. (3) Wholesale wool and yarn costs have risen 8.6% year-on-year, consumer spending on online knitwear grew 4.1%, and inflation is running at 5.9%.

questions.question_text: TWF plans to fund part of its $560,000 expansion with a $360,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TWF of using $200,000 retained profit instead.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs TWF nothing in interest or capital repayments, so the $200,000 finances a new e-commerce returns and yarn-refurbishment hub without increasing the $360,000 debt commitment. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 8.6% rise in wool and yarn input costs named in Appendix 3, protecting the $4.80 contribution per unit earned on each of the 78,000 units sold.

Point 2: Retaining profit leaves ownership and control with Beatrix Fenn and the existing owners, so no bank can impose conditions on how the $560,000 investment is run. It is also flexible: with 52 staff and a laissez-faire leadership style, TWF can time spending on the new facility to match cash generation. A bank loan would require regular interest and eventual repayment, which would strain cash flow if knitwear e-commerce retail demand weakened during the expansion.

Taken together, the $200,000 funds a new e-commerce returns and yarn-refurbishment hub without competing with the $360,000 debt service, leaving the $144,000 of annual fixed costs to be covered by the $4.80 contribution on each of the 78,000 units. In knitwear e-commerce retail, where the 8.6% input-cost rise already pressures margins, avoiding compulsory interest payments gives TWF a materially safer route than increasing its borrowings for a flat organisation with 52 staff.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to Threadwind Fashion and its financing choice.

questions.question_text: TWF is promoting its knitwear e-commerce retail offering. Consider paid search advertising, fashion blogger collaborations, or local radio advertising. Which should TWF choose to promote its online knitwear brand? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Paid search advertising: Search advertising catches knitwear buyers exactly when they are looking to purchase, delivering measurable traffic to the online store. Keywords can be expensive and traffic ends when the budget ends, so it may not build the long-term brand that a $560,000 returns hub needs.

Fashion blogger collaborations: Bloggers and reviewers provide credible product demonstrations and can reach the 54%% of surveyed buyers who read reviews before ordering. This is cost-effective and on-message for knitwear, but results depend on the blogger's audience and reputation and are harder to scale quickly.

Local radio advertising: Radio is cheaper than national digital or print media and suits a time-limited knitwear offer, but its reach is geographically narrow and TWF sells online to a national market, so most listeners would not be customers.

Recommendation: TWF should choose fashion blogger collaborations. They deliver the credibility that matters to the 54%% of surveyed knitwear buyers who read reviews, at low and controllable cost, which suits a partnership funding a $560,000 hub. Paid search is rejected because its traffic stops when spending stops, and local radio is rejected because the online knitwear market is national, not local.

With fixed costs of $144,000 a year and a $360,000 loan to service, TWF needs volume at a controlled cost, so the chosen method must reach buyers who will actually convert; that is why the two rejected options, despite their superficial appeal, are set aside in favour of the more targeted approach. The decision should be reviewed against the sales and enquiry figures in Appendix 1 after one campaign cycle, and the spend justified only if the extra orders cover the $4.80 contribution needed toward the $144,000 fixed costs of the knitwear e-commerce retail business.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of promotional methods with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of the business with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of Threadwind Fashion with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the two rejected options lose.

questions.question_text: TWF faces 38 quality complaints a month and absenteeism of 8.5%. Explain two benefits for TWF of using laissez-faire leadership in its design and packing teams.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives the design and packing teams freedom to experiment with yarn choices and returns handling, which can generate the ideas needed to solve the 38 pilling complaints a month. With a flat structure and 52 staff, self-directed employees can respond faster to quality problems than a distant manager.

Point 2: Delegation raises ownership of decisions, which can improve morale and reduce the 8.5% absenteeism the business faces, while experienced packers take responsibility for inducting colleagues on the new scanner. Beatrix Fenn must set clear quality standards, because too little direction could let defects rise; used with clear targets, laissez-faire leadership supports the $560,000 refurbishment hub and protects the 78,000-unit output.

These benefits matter because fixed costs of $144,000 mean TWF must keep output close to 78,000 units a year; every experienced worker lost through turnover or absence is replaced at a retraining cost shown in Appendix 1, and a destabilised team would slow the $560,000 rollout. Better motivation therefore protects the quality figures reported in Appendix 1 and the $4.80 contribution on each unit, which is what allows the partnership to absorb the 8.6% rise in wool and yarn costs without cutting the 78,000-unit plan.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to Threadwind Fashion's problem, costs and output.

questions.question_text: TWF must train staff to use its new equipment. Consider on-the-job induction on the new returns scanner or external e-learning at $60 per employee. Which should TWF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job induction on the returns scanner: Hands-on training at the returns desk is specific to TWF's own scanner, costs no fee, and keeps the 14 staff productive while learning, protecting the 78,000-unit output and the response to 38 monthly complaints. Trainers are colleagues whose work suffers and there is no formal record, which matters for a partnership with a $560,000 hub.

External e-learning at $60 per employee: Consistent online modules give a completion record for all 14 staff at a total cost of 14 Ã— $60 = $840, negligible against the $560,000 investment. Content may be generic and training time reduces short-term packing capacity, especially with 8.5% absenteeism.

Decision: TWF should choose on-the-job induction for immediate scanner skills, supplemented by e-learning for records. On-the-job training is cheapest and tailored to the new hub; e-learning alone is rejected because generic modules cannot teach the exact returns process and would lose packing hours when absenteeism already runs at 8.5%.

The wider context reinforces this decision. With fixed costs of $144,000 and the $360,000 loan to service, TWF cannot afford the output loss that follows withdrawing the staff concerned from the line for long. The documented problem in Appendix 1 â€” the defect and turnover figures â€” makes early practical competence on the actual equipment more valuable than a generic certificate. A short external top-up later can add formal recognition without the disruption of full off-the-job training, so the chosen blend protects both the 78,000-unit volume and the quality the partnership is trying to improve as it invests $560,000 in new knitwear e-commerce retail capacity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to the business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of the business.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of Threadwind Fashion with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TWF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs Ã· Contribution per unit. Substitution: $144,000 Ã· ($11.00 âˆ’ $6.20) = $144,000 Ã· $4.80 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price âˆ’ Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $11.00 âˆ’ $6.20 = $4.80. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.80.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TWF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 78,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 48,000 units, to judge whether the $560,000 investment is safely profitable.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.80 lets managers model a discount: for example a 5% cut in the $11.00 selling price would lower contribution and show the extra volume needed to cover $144,000 fixed costs.
3. With $144,000 fixed costs and $4.80 contribution, managers can set the sales volumes needed to service the $360,000 loan before committing further capital to a new e-commerce returns and yarn-refurbishment hub.
4. Unit cost of about $8.05 ($144,000 Ã· 78,000 units + $6.20) can be benchmarked each quarter to spot waste from the wool and yarn cost inflation of 8.6% and to check whether the $6.20 variable cost can be renegotiated. Together these figures guide pricing, volume and cost control at TWF.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.80 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 48,000 units against 78,000 output; pricing/discount modelling against $144,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume for the $560,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at about $8.05 to tackle 8.6% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TWF's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TWF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.29 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.42 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.69 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $76 inventories + $48 trade receivables + $18 cash = $142; 2025 current assets = $92 + $52 + $34 = $178. Dividing by current liabilities of $110 (2024) and $125 (2025) gives the 2024 figure of 1.29 and the 2025 figure of 1.42. For the second measure, (current assets âˆ’ inventories) Ã· current liabilities gives 2024: ($142 âˆ’ $76) Ã· $110 = $66 Ã· $110 = 0.60; 2025: ($178 âˆ’ $92) Ã· $125 = $86 Ã· $125 = 0.69.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. The 2024 coverage of 1.29 rose to 1.42 in 2025, meaning current assets cover short-term obligations more comfortably, helped by current liabilities falling from $110 to $125. The stricter measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.60 to 0.69, so TWF is less dependent on selling stock to meet debts â€” important while it services a $360,000 loan and funds a $560,000 expansion. Trade receivables moved from $48 to $52, tying up cash that could be slower to collect, and inventories moved from $76 to $92, so availability for peak demand should still be watched. Non-current assets grew from $980 to $1,300, consistent with the new investment, while capital employed rose from $1,120 to $1,400.

Conclusion: TWF's financial position has improved. Both short-term solvency measures rose (1.29 to 1.42 and 0.60 to 0.69) and the improvement does not rely on inventory alone. The main residual risk is the $52 of trade receivables, so tighter credit control is advisable before further expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether Threadwind Fashion's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TWF of switching to guaranteed non-pilling yarn for its knitwear.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Guaranteed non-pilling yarn answers the pilling complaints that have reached 38 a month, and the 66% of surveyed buyers would pay $54% more for it, so TWF can charge a premium that lifts the $4.80 contribution per unit.

Disadvantage: Better yarn raises the $6.20 variable cost, and with wool and yarn costs already up 8.6% the margin could be squeezed. If the guarantee is not trusted despite 54%% reading reviews, the extra cost may not be recovered.

Managers should set the premium against the $4.80 contribution per unit and the $144,000 annual fixed costs: the survey evidence in Appendix 1 suggests customers will pay more, but the 8.6% rise in wool and yarn costs and the need to sustain 78,000 units mean the net gain must be checked. If volumes fall, the extra cost would not be recovered, so the effect should be reviewed after one quarter. For a partnership with 52 staff, the change also affects training and the brand Beatrix Fenn has built, so it belongs alongside the service and quality improvements already reported in Appendix 1 rather than being introduced in isolation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to Threadwind Fashion's data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.50%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 8.6% rise in wool and yarn input costs will affect TWF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): The insert states TWF has a $360,000 bank loan. A rise of 0.75 percentage points adds 0.75% Ã— $360,000 = $2,700 a year if the loan is variable-rate; if the rate is fixed, the direct effect is nil. Higher base rates could also raise the cost of future borrowing for the $560,000 expansion and make consumers more cautious about knitwear e-commerce retail spending.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.50 per hour): With a workforce of 52, this raises wage costs in the partly hourly-paid fulfilment and store roles. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no defensible annual wage bill can be invented. The only honest yardstick is the productivity already derivable: 78,000 units Ã· 52 staff = 1,500 units per worker. A wage rise is absorbable only if productivity holds near that level or output grows, otherwise unit labour costs rise and the $4.80 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (8.6% in wool and yarn): TWF's variable cost is $6.20 a unit and the insert does not decompose it, so the only defensible bound is to apply the full rise: 8.6% Ã— $6.20 = $0.533 a unit, which at 78,000 units is about $41,589.60 a year (78,000 Ã— $0.533). Even a smaller effect would cut the $4.80 contribution and threaten the $560,000 investment; the $54% premium from the survey can recover only part of it.

Conclusion: The 8.6% rise in wool and yarn costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 78,000 units sold, directly erodes the $4.80 contribution that justifies the $560,000 expansion, and is only partly offset by the premium. The interest rise is smaller ($2,700 at most, and possibly nil), and the wage impact, though unavoidable, can be managed through the 1,500-unit productivity the business already achieves.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of Threadwind Fashion with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
